key_terms.meaning: The three normal stresses on mutually perpendicular planes where the shear stress is zero; every failure theory starts from them.
A single uniaxial stress that would fail the part at the same instant as the real combined stress state; compare it with S<sub>yt</sub> or S<sub>ut</sub>.

Brittle-material theory: failure when σ<sub>1</sub> reaches S<sub>ut</sub> in tension or σ<sub>3</sub> reaches −S<sub>uc</sub> in compression; safe if σ<sub>1</sub> ≤ S<sub>ut</sub>/n and |σ<sub>3</sub>| ≤ S<sub>uc</sub>/n.
Failure when τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)/2 reaches S<sub>sy</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>/2, so safe if σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> ≤ S<sub>yt</sub>/n.
Failure when the distortion part of the strain energy reaches its value at yield: σ<sub>eq</sub> = √(σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>²) ≤ S<sub>yt</sub>/n.
Failure when the largest principal strain reaches the strain at yield: safe if σ<sub>1</sub> − ν(σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>) ≤ S<sub>yt</sub>/n, with ν the Poisson ratio; rarely used now.
Brittle-material theory with different tensile and compressive strengths; safe if σ<sub>1</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>/S<sub>uc</sub> ≤ 1/n, with compression negative.

Failure when the total strain energy per unit volume reaches its value at yield: σ<sub>1</sub>² + σ<sub>2</sub>² + σ<sub>3</sub>² − 2ν(σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>σ<sub>3</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>σ<sub>1</sub>) ≤ (S<sub>yt</sub>/n)².

K<sub>t</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>nom</sub>, the rise of the peak local elastic stress at a hole, groove or fillet over the nominal net-section stress; it depends on geometry and load type, not on the material.
q = (K<sub>f</sub> − 1)/(K<sub>t</sub> − 1); q = 0 for a material that ignores the notch and q = 1 when the full theoretical rise is felt.
K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1), the reduced concentration actually used on the alternating stress in a fatigue check.
Progressive cracking of a part under repeated or fluctuating stress whose peak may stay well below the yield strength.
A plot of stress amplitude S in MPa against the number of cycles to failure N, drawn on log–log axes; for steels it levels off into a horizontal line.

The fully reversed stress amplitude below which a steel survives indefinitely, taken at the knee of the S–N curve (10⁶ cycles; some books 10⁷). For a real part S<sub>e</sub> = k<sub>a</sub> k<sub>b</sub> k<sub>c</sub> k<sub>d</sub> k<sub>e</sub> Se′.
The stress amplitude that gives a stated finite life of N cycles, read off the sloping part of the S–N curve.
Cumulative damage: a part fails when Σ n<sub>i</sub>/N<sub>i</sub> = 1, where n<sub>i</sub> cycles are applied at a level whose life is N<sub>i</sub>.
σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> + σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, the steady part of a fluctuating stress cycle.
σ<sub>a</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, the half-range of the cycle that drives the fatigue damage.
σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>yt</sub> = 1; a straight failure line that is the most conservative of the three common criteria.
σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> = 1; the straight line joining S<sub>e</sub> on the alternating axis to S<sub>ut</sub> on the mean axis.
σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + (σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub>)² = 1; a parabola through the same two points that fits test data on ductile metals best.
σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>, the first-cycle yield check that must accompany the Gerber and Goodman lines.
The ratio of the maximum dynamic stress or deflection to the static value under the same load: 2 for a suddenly applied load and 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>) for a weight dropped through a height h.

takeaways: A theory of failure replaces the whole combined stress state by one equivalent stress; ductile parts are checked against S<sub>yt</sub>, brittle parts against S<sub>ut</sub> and S<sub>uc</sub>.
Tresca's hexagon lies inside the von Mises ellipse, so Tresca is the safer of the two; they differ most in pure shear, 0.5S<sub>yt</sub> against 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>.
A hole or fillet raises the local stress by K<sub>t</sub>, but under repeated load the material feels only K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1).
Fatigue cracks start at a surface stress raiser at stresses well below yield, so a generous fillet and a smooth or peened surface add more life than extra material.
For steel the S–N line runs from 0.9S<sub>ut</sub> at 10³ cycles to S<sub>e</sub> at 10⁶ cycles; the same line gives the life at any amplitude in between, and Miner's rule adds up mixed levels.
Marin's factors turn the test-bar endurance limit 0.5S<sub>ut</sub> into the endurance limit of the real part.
A mean stress lowers the allowable amplitude: Soderberg is the most conservative line, Goodman the usual design line, Gerber the closest to tests, and Gerber and Goodman need the Langer yield check.
A weight dropped through a height must be stopped by strain energy, W(h + δ) = ½kδ², so a stiff part feels a very large impact factor and a soft cushion lowers it.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit pair a statement or derivation with a numerical check, so expect marks for the correct equivalent stress or stress components, the correct failure line, the numbers worked to a factor of safety or a size, and a closing comment on which criterion is conservative and why.

bank.q: State the theories of failure, write the failure condition of each in terms of the principal stresses, and explain why the distortion energy theory is preferred for ductile metals.
outline: principal stresses σ<sub>1</sub> ≥ σ<sub>2</sub> ≥ σ<sub>3</sub>
Rankine: σ<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>ut</sub> (or σ<sub>3</sub> = −S<sub>uc</sub>)
Tresca: σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>
St Venant: σ<sub>1</sub> − ν(σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>) = S<sub>yt</sub>
Haigh: total strain energy at yield
von Mises: ½[(σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>)² + (σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)² + (σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>)²] = S<sub>yt</sub>²
hydrostatic stress does not cause yield; von Mises leaves it out
pure shear check: 0.577S<sub>yt</sub> against tests

answer.text: Set up. At the critical point find the principal stresses and order them σ<sub>1</sub> ≥ σ<sub>2</sub> ≥ σ<sub>3</sub> (tension positive). A tensile test gives one strength: S<sub>yt</sub> for a ductile metal, S<sub>ut</sub> (and S<sub>uc</sub> in compression) for a brittle one. Each theory says which quantity, when it reaches its value in the tensile test, causes failure. With a factor of safety n the limit is divided by n.

Maximum principal stress theory (Rankine). Failure when the largest principal stress reaches the strength: σ<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>ut</sub> in tension or σ<sub>3</sub> = −S<sub>uc</sub> in compression. It ignores shear, so it suits brittle materials, which fail by separation.

Maximum shear stress theory (Tresca, Guest). Failure when τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)/2 reaches the shear stress at yield in the tensile test, S<sub>yt</sub>/2. So σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>, and the shear yield strength is S<sub>sy</sub> = 0.5S<sub>yt</sub>.

Maximum principal strain theory (St Venant). Failure when the largest strain reaches the yield strain S<sub>yt</sub>/E: σ<sub>1</sub> − ν(σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>) = S<sub>yt</sub>. It fits test data poorly and is rarely used.

Maximum strain energy theory (Haigh). Failure when the strain energy per unit volume reaches its value at yield, S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E): σ<sub>1</sub>² + σ<sub>2</sub>² + σ<sub>3</sub>² − 2ν(σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>σ<sub>3</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>σ<sub>1</sub>) = S<sub>yt</sub>². It wrongly predicts that a large hydrostatic pressure alone causes yield.

Maximum distortion energy theory (von Mises, Hencky). The strain energy is split into a volume-change part and a shape-change (distortion) part; failure when the distortion part reaches its value at yield:
answer.pre:
½[(σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>)² + (σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)² + (σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>)²] = S<sub>yt</sub>²
plane stress (σ<sub>3</sub> = 0):  σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>² = S<sub>yt</sub>²

answer.text: Coulomb–Mohr, for brittle materials with S<sub>uc</sub> > S<sub>ut</sub>: σ<sub>1</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>/S<sub>uc</sub> = 1 with σ<sub>3</sub> negative.

Why von Mises for ductile metals. (a) Ductile metals yield by shear slip, which changes shape, not volume. A hydrostatic stress (σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>2</sub> = σ<sub>3</sub>) gives zero distortion energy and, in tests, causes no yield; von Mises is the only theory above that leaves it out completely. (b) In pure shear (σ<sub>1</sub> = τ, σ<sub>2</sub> = 0, σ<sub>3</sub> = −τ) von Mises gives √3 τ = S<sub>yt</sub>, so S<sub>sy</sub> = 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>, and torsion tests on steels give about 0.55 to 0.6S<sub>yt</sub>. Tresca's 0.5S<sub>yt</sub> is on the safe side; Rankine's S<sub>sy</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub> is unsafe.
Summary table.

Closing check with numbers. For σ<sub>x</sub> = 100, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40, τ<sub>xy</sub> = 60 MPa (σ<sub>1</sub> = 137.08, σ<sub>2</sub> = 2.92, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0) and S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa: Tresca n = 400/137.08 = 2.92, von Mises n = 400/135.65 = 2.95. The two agree near the corners of the hexagon and differ by up to 15 % in shear, so von Mises is preferred for analysis and Tresca where a simple, safe answer is enough.

bank.q: Explain why one failure theory cannot serve both ductile and brittle materials. Use the shape of the tensile test curve, the type of fracture and the effect of hydrostatic stress in your answer.
outline: ductile: yielding by shear, large plastic strain before fracture
brittle: separation with little or no plasticity
hydrostatic stress changes volume but not shape, so it does not yield a ductile metal
hydrostatic compression strengthens a brittle material
Coulomb–Mohr needed when S<sub>uc</sub> differs from S<sub>ut</sub>
design comparison: against S<sub>yt</sub> or against S<sub>ut</sub>

answer.text: The tensile test shows the difference. A ductile steel yields at S<sub>yt</sub>, then stretches plastically (often 20 % or more) before it fractures at a necked, cup-and-cone surface. A brittle cast iron shows almost no plastic strain and breaks at S<sub>ut</sub> on a flat face normal to the load.

So the two materials fail by different mechanisms. Ductile failure begins with yielding, which is slip on planes of maximum shear; the useful limit is S<sub>yt</sub> and the right theories are shear or distortion theories (Tresca, von Mises). Brittle failure is separation by normal stress at flaws; the limit is S<sub>ut</sub> and the right theories are normal-stress theories (Rankine, Coulomb–Mohr).

Hydrostatic stress. Equal stresses on three planes change volume but not shape, so they cannot drive slip: a ductile metal under high hydrostatic pressure does not yield, and von Mises (which ignores the hydrostatic part) predicts exactly this. A brittle material, by contrast, is much stronger when its flaws are squeezed shut: hydrostatic compression strengthens it, and its compressive strength S<sub>uc</sub> is often three to four times S<sub>ut</sub>.

Unequal tension and compression strengths. Because S<sub>uc</sub> ≠ S<sub>ut</sub> for cast iron, a theory with one strength cannot fit both sides; Coulomb–Mohr uses both: σ<sub>1</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>/S<sub>uc</sub> = 1/n.
Design comparison.

How to choose in an exam answer. First decide the material class from its elongation: more than about 5 % elongation in the tensile test means ductile, less means brittle. Then pick the strength that matches the failure mode (yield for ductile, ultimate for brittle) and the theory built on the same cause. Writing the wrong strength with the right theory, for example S<sub>ut</sub> with von Mises for a mild steel part, loses the marks for the method even when the arithmetic is correct.

A borderline case. Some materials sit between the classes: a nodular cast iron with 10 % elongation is treated as ductile, a grey cast iron with under 1 % as brittle. A ductile steel can also behave in a brittle way at low temperature, under impact, or with a sharp crack under high triaxial tension, which is why fracture mechanics is used for such cases.

Numerical check. A cast iron bracket with S<sub>ut</sub> = 200 MPa, S<sub>uc</sub> = 600 MPa and principal stresses 50 and −150 MPa: Coulomb–Mohr gives 1/n = 50/200 + 150/600 = 0.50, n = 2.0. Treated wrongly as ductile with von Mises against 200 MPa, σ<sub>eq</sub> = √(50² + 50 × 150 + 150²) = 180.3 MPa and n = 1.11, which misjudges the part because it ignores the higher compressive strength. One theory cannot serve both materials.

bank.q: Define stress concentration factor K<sub>t</sub> and notch sensitivity q. Show that the fatigue notch factor is K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1), and state the material and geometric factors on which q depends.
outline: K<sub>t</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>nom</sub> from charts, photoelasticity or finite elements
K<sub>t</sub> depends on geometry and load type, not on material
q = (K<sub>f</sub> − 1)/(K<sub>t</sub> − 1)
rearrange to K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1)
q rises with notch radius and with tensile strength (finer-grained, stronger steels)
q about 0.2 for grey cast iron, close to 1 for hardened steel unless the radius is very small

answer.text: Stress concentration factor. At a hole, groove or fillet the elastic stress rises to a local peak σ<sub>max</sub> above the nominal stress σ<sub>nom</sub> computed on the net section. K<sub>t</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>nom</sub>. It is found from Peterson-type charts (against D/d and r/d), photoelasticity or finite element analysis. Being an elastic result, it depends only on the shape and on whether the load is axial, bending or torsion.

Fatigue notch factor. Fatigue tests on notched and smooth bars of the same material give K<sub>f</sub> = (endurance limit of the smooth bar)/(endurance limit of the notched bar). Tests show K<sub>f</sub> ≤ K<sub>t</sub>, because at a small notch the stress falls steeply away from the root and the material around helps the stressed grains.
Notch sensitivity. q measures what fraction of the theoretical rise above 1 is felt in fatigue:

Rearranging: q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1) = K<sub>f</sub> − 1, so K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1). With q = 0, K<sub>f</sub> = 1 (notch has no effect); with q = 1, K<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> (full effect).

What q depends on. Material: stronger, finer-grained steels have a smaller Neuber constant √a and so a higher q; grey cast iron already contains graphite flakes that act as internal notches, so an external notch adds little and q ≈ 0.2. Geometry: q rises with the notch radius r. Neuber's estimate q = 1/(1 + √a/√r) shows both trends.
Numbers for a 600 MPa steel in bending, √a = 0.38 √mm:

Use in design. K<sub>f</sub> multiplies the alternating nominal stress (or divides the endurance limit, but not both); K<sub>t</sub> is used for a brittle part under static load; a ductile part under static load is normally designed on the nominal stress because local yielding relieves the peak.

Closing check. For the stepped shaft of the stress concentration chapter (σ<sub>nom</sub> = 47.75 MPa, K<sub>t</sub> = 1.6, q = 0.84): peak 76.4 MPa, K<sub>f</sub> = 1.50 and the fatigue check uses 71.8 MPa, between σ<sub>nom</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub> as the definition requires.

bank.q: Describe the mechanism of fatigue failure in a metal part, covering crack initiation, stage I and stage II growth, and final fracture, and state where the crack usually starts.
outline: cyclic slip in persistent slip bands on the surface
initiation at a stress raiser, inclusion or machining mark
stage I growth along slip planes, slow and shallow
stage II growth normal to the load, one striation per cycle
beach marks show the crack front position
final fast fracture when the remaining ligament cannot carry the load
most cracks start at a free surface

answer.text: Definition. Fatigue is the progressive growth of a crack under repeated or fluctuating stress, ending in sudden fracture, at stresses that may be well below the yield strength. It accounts for most service failures of shafts, axles, springs and bolts.

Crack initiation. Even below yield, a few favourably oriented surface grains slip back and forth each cycle. The slip concentrates in persistent slip bands, which push out tiny extrusions and intrusions on the surface; an intrusion is a micro-notch from which a crack starts. Initiation is fastest where the local stress is highest: at fillets, keyways, thread roots, holes, machining marks, inclusions, corrosion pits and decarburised skins. Most cracks start at a free surface, because the bending and torsion stresses are largest there and the surface carries the flaws.
Stage I growth. The new crack grows a few grains deep along the active slip planes, at about 45° to the load, very slowly. It is shallow and hard to see.

Stage II growth. The crack turns to run normal to the largest tensile stress and grows by a small step each cycle: the tip opens and blunts on loading and resharpens on unloading. Each step leaves a striation, visible only under an electron microscope. Changes in load or pauses leave beach marks (clamshell marks), curved lines visible to the eye that show the successive positions of the crack front and point back to the origin.

Final fracture. The uncracked ligament shrinks until it can no longer carry the peak load; it then breaks in one cycle by ductile overload or brittle fracture. The fracture face therefore has two zones.

head: Zone
Appearance
Tells you
rows: smooth, beach marks, origin at the surface
where and how slowly the crack grew
the load at the end; a large zone means a high stress

answer.text: Design consequences. Because cracks start at surface stress raisers, life is improved by generous fillets, a fine finish, shot peening or surface rolling (residual compression), and by avoiding corrosion; extra cross-section helps less.

Closing check. For the machined 600 MPa shaft of the fatigue chapter (S<sub>e</sub> = 230 MPa), an amplitude of 300 MPa, half the ultimate strength, still gives only 1.16 × 10⁵ cycles: well below yield, yet a finite life.

bank.q: Draw a typical S–N curve for steel and explain its shape. Define endurance limit and fatigue strength, and list the factors that make the endurance limit of a real component lower than that of a polished laboratory specimen.
outline: log S against log N, low-cycle (< 10³) and high-cycle regions
0.9S<sub>ut</sub> at 10³ cycles, knee at 10⁶ (some books 10⁷) for steel
S<sub>e</sub> is the plateau, S<sub>f</sub> the value at a stated life
non-ferrous metals show no plateau
Marin factors: surface, size, load, temperature, reliability
notch through K<sub>f</sub>

answer.text: The test. Polished specimens are run on an R. R. Moore rotating-beam machine at several fully reversed stress amplitudes S, and the cycles to failure N are recorded. S is plotted against N on log–log axes.

Shape for steel (sketch: a falling straight line, then a horizontal line). Up to about 10³ cycles is low-cycle fatigue, where the stress is near S<sub>ut</sub> and design is treated as static. From 10³ to 10⁶ cycles the points lie close to a straight line from 0.9S<sub>ut</sub> to S<sub>e</sub>: the finite-life region. At about 10⁶ cycles the line bends into a horizontal plateau (the knee); below the plateau the steel does not fail however many cycles it sees.

Definitions. Endurance limit S<sub>e</sub>: the plateau stress, the fully reversed amplitude a steel can carry indefinitely. Fatigue strength S<sub>f</sub>: the amplitude that gives a stated life N, read on the sloping line, for example S<sub>f</sub> at 10⁵ cycles. Aluminium and copper alloys have no plateau, so only S<sub>f</sub> at a stated life (often 5 × 10⁸ cycles) can be quoted.
Numbers for S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa, S<sub>e</sub> = 230 MPa:

Why a real part is weaker than the test bar. Se′ ≈ 0.5S<sub>ut</sub> is measured on a small polished bar in rotating bending at room temperature, with 50 % survival. Each difference costs strength and has a Marin factor: S<sub>e</sub> = k<sub>a</sub> k<sub>b</sub> k<sub>c</sub> k<sub>d</sub> k<sub>e</sub> Se′.
The factors.

head: Factor
Reason
Typical value
rows: machining marks and scale start cracks
a larger stressed volume holds more flaws
axial load stresses the whole section; torsion uses shear strength

answer.text: Stress concentration enters through K<sub>f</sub>, either multiplying the stress amplitude or as a factor 1/K<sub>f</sub> on S<sub>e</sub>, never both.

Closing check. S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa: Se′ = 300 MPa; k<sub>a</sub> = 0.85, k<sub>b</sub> = 0.90 give S<sub>e</sub> = 229.5 ≈ 230 MPa, only 77 % of the test-bar value, and the 300 MPa amplitude that a test bar would survive indefinitely gives the real shaft about 1.16 × 10⁵ cycles.

bank.q: A solid circular shaft of 50 mm diameter carries a bending moment of 800 N·m and a torque of 600 N·m. The material has yield strength 350 MPa. Find the factor of safety by the maximum shear stress theory and by the distortion energy theory, and comment on the difference.
outline: σ = 32M/(πd³) and τ = 16T/(πd³)
principal stresses σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²); one is negative, so order them σ<sub>1</sub>, 0, σ<sub>3</sub>
Tresca: n = S<sub>yt</sub>/(σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)
von Mises: σ<sub>eq</sub> = √(σ² + 3τ²), n = S<sub>yt</sub>/σ<sub>eq</sub>
Tresca gives the smaller n
the gap is small here because bending dominates; it reaches about 15 % only in pure shear

answer.text: Data: d = 50 mm, M = 800 N·m = 800 000 N·mm, T = 600 N·m = 600 000 N·mm, S<sub>yt</sub> = 350 MPa. The critical point is on the surface, where both stresses are largest.
Stresses: d³ = 125 000 mm³.
Principal stresses (plane stress, σ<sub>y</sub> = 0):
Order them: σ<sub>1</sub> = 73.34 MPa, σ<sub>2</sub> = 0, σ<sub>3</sub> = −8.15 MPa. The zero stress is the middle one because one in-plane stress is negative.
Maximum shear stress theory: σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = 73.34 − (−8.15) = 81.49 MPa (equal to 2 × 40.74, twice the circle radius). n = 350/81.49 = 4.30.
Distortion energy theory, straight from the loads:
Check from the principal stresses: √(σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>3</sub> + σ<sub>3</sub>²) = √(73.34² + 73.34 × 8.15 + 8.15²) = √(5378.8 + 597.7 + 66.4) = √6042.9 = 77.74 MPa, the same.

Method in words. The surface point of a shaft under bending and torsion is in plane stress: a normal stress from bending along the axis, a shear stress from torsion on the same faces, and nothing on the free surface. Both theories need the principal stresses or, for von Mises, the shortcut σ<sub>eq</sub> = √(σ² + 3τ²), which comes from putting Mohr's circle into the distortion energy expression.

Equivalent moments, the shaft-design form. The same results follow from equivalent moments. Tresca: T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) = √(800² + 600²) = 1000 N·m, so τ<sub>max</sub> = 16 × 1 000 000/(π × 125 000) = 40.74 MPa, the circle radius found above, and n = 175/40.74 = 4.30. Von Mises: M<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + 0.75T²) = √(640 000 + 270 000) = 953.9 N·m, so σ<sub>eq</sub> = 32 × 953 900/(π × 125 000) = 77.74 MPa, as above.

Comment. Tresca gives n = 4.30, von Mises 4.50: Tresca is about 4.7 % more conservative. The difference is small because bending dominates (σ is 2.7 times τ), so the point lies near a corner of the hexagon where the two boundaries meet; in pure torsion the difference would grow to 15 %. Both show the shaft is safe with a good margin; a designer could use a smaller shaft.

bank.q: A flat steel plate 10 mm thick and 100 mm wide has a central circular hole of 20 mm diameter and carries an axial pull of 60 kN. Taking K<sub>t</sub> = 2.5 from the chart and q = 0.85, find the nominal stress, the peak stress and the fatigue notch factor, and comment on the result.
outline: nominal stress on the net section: σ<sub>nom</sub> = P/((w − d)t)
peak stress σ<sub>max</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub>
K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1)
net, not gross, section
the peak is local and dies out within about one hole diameter

answer.text: Net area at the hole: A<sub>net</sub> = (w − d)t = (100 − 20) × 10 = 800 mm².
Nominal stress: σ<sub>nom</sub> = 60 000/800 = 75.0 MPa. (On the gross area 1000 mm² it would be 60 MPa; the chart's K<sub>t</sub> was drawn for the net section, so 75 MPa is the value to use.)
Check the chart value: d/w = 0.2, and Heywood's formula gives K<sub>t</sub> = 2 + (1 − 0.2)³ = 2.51, in agreement with 2.5.
Peak stress at the edge of the hole: σ<sub>max</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub> = 2.5 × 75.0 = 187.5 MPa.
Fatigue notch factor: K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1) = 1 + 0.85 × (2.5 − 1) = 1 + 1.275 = 2.275.
Results.

Why the net section. K<sub>t</sub> charts for a plate with a hole are drawn with σ<sub>nom</sub> on the reduced section through the hole, because that is the section the load must pass through; a chart drawn on the gross section exists too, with larger K<sub>t</sub> values. Mixing the two gives a peak 20 % too low here (2.5 × 60 = 150 instead of 187.5 MPa).

Where q comes from. q = 0.85 is a typical value for a medium-carbon steel at a hole radius of 10 mm; data books give q against notch radius for each class of steel, and Neuber's formula q = 1/(1 + √a/√r) gives a similar value.

Comment. The peak acts only at the edge of the hole and falls to near the nominal value within about one hole diameter. Under a steady pull a ductile steel plate would yield locally and redistribute it, so static design can use 75 MPa. If the 60 kN load repeats, fatigue sees 2.28 × 75 = 170.6 MPa, more than twice the nominal stress, so the hole, not the plate's width, decides its fatigue design. A brittle plate would need the full 187.5 MPa even under static load.

bank.q: A steel component has S<sub>ut</sub> = 650 MPa, S<sub>yt</sub> = 520 MPa and a completely reversed endurance limit S<sub>e</sub> = 240 MPa. It works at σ<sub>m</sub> = 120 MPa and σ<sub>a</sub> = 150 MPa. Check the safety by the Soderberg, Goodman and Gerber criteria and state which one is most conservative.
outline: Soderberg: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>yt</sub> = 1/n
Goodman: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> = 1/n
Gerber: n σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + (n σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub>)² = 1 (quadratic in n)
Langer yield check n = S<sub>yt</sub>/(σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>)
Soderberg gives the lowest n
Gerber closest to ductile test data

answer.text: Data: S<sub>ut</sub> = 650 MPa, S<sub>yt</sub> = 520 MPa, S<sub>e</sub> = 240 MPa, σ<sub>m</sub> = 120 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 150 MPa. The two terms used throughout: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> = 150/240 = 0.6250.
Soderberg:
Goodman:
Gerber: scale both stresses by n and put them on the parabola:
Yield (Langer) check: σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = 270 MPa, n = 520/270 = 1.93. All three fatigue values are below 1.93, so fatigue, not yield, governs in every case.
Summary.

Method. The three criteria differ only in the line on the Haigh diagram. For each, the working point (σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub>) = (120, 150) is scaled by n along the line from the origin until it meets the failure line. For the straight lines this gives 1/n directly as the sum of two ratios; for the Gerber parabola, the scaled point (nσm, nσa) is put into the parabola, giving a quadratic in n.

Reading the answer on the diagram. The working point sits at σ<sub>a</sub>/σ<sub>m</sub> = 1.25, a steep ray. It reaches Soderberg first, at (140, 175), then Goodman at (148, 185) and Gerber at (178, 222) MPa, all well inside the Langer line at (231, 289). This is why fatigue governs here: the alternating part is large compared with the mean.

Comment. Soderberg is the most conservative because its line ends at S<sub>yt</sub> < S<sub>ut</sub>; Gerber gives the largest n because its parabola bows outside the Goodman straight line, closest to test data. All three exceed 1, so the part is safe, but by Soderberg and Goodman the margin (17 to 24 %) is thin for a machine part; a designer would want about 1.5, which would need a lower stress or a higher S<sub>e</sub> (better finish, larger fillet).

bank.q: A weight of 500 N is dropped through a height of 40 mm on to a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel rod 20 mm diameter and 1.5 m long, with E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum stress in the rod and the impact factor.
outline: static extension δ<sub>st</sub> = WL/(AE)
energy balance W(h + δ) = ½Pδ
dynamic extension δ = δ<sub>st</sub>(1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>))
impact factor = δ/δ<sub>st</sub>
σ<sub>max</sub> = impact factor × σ<sub>st</sub>
state assumptions: elastic impact, no energy lost, mass of rod neglected

answer.text: Data: W = 500 N, h = 40 mm, d = 20 mm, L = 1.5 m = 1500 mm, E = 200 GPa = 200 000 N/mm². Area A = π × 20²/4 = 314.16 mm².
Static extension and stress:

Energy balance. The weight falls h and then a further δ while the rod stretches, so the work W(h + δ) equals the strain energy ½(AE/L)δ². With δ<sub>st</sub> = WL/(AE) this is δ² − 2δ<sub>st</sub> δ − 2hδst = 0, whose positive root is δ = δ<sub>st</sub>(1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>)).
Impact factor:
Maximum extension and stress:

Assumptions: the rod stays elastic (131.9 MPa is below the yield of mild steel, about 250 MPa); no energy is lost as heat, sound or local plastic flow at the collar; the rod's mass is neglected; the stress is uniform along the rod at every instant.

Why the work is W(h + δ), not Wh. At the moment of impact the weight has kinetic energy Wh. It keeps moving down while the rod stretches, losing a further Wδ of potential energy. At maximum extension it is momentarily at rest, so both parts are stored as strain energy. Leaving out Wδ gives δ = √(2hδst) = 0.977 mm, about 1 % low here, but badly wrong for short drops.

Comment. The drop multiplies the stress 83 times. Compared with a 1 m rod and a 50 mm drop (180 MPa in the impact chapter), the longer rod is more flexible (larger δ<sub>st</sub>), so it feels a smaller stress even though it is the same diameter: in impact, flexibility protects.

bank.q: A stepped shaft has a fillet with K<sub>t</sub> = 2.2, and the material has q = 0.9, S<sub>e</sub> = 220 MPa, S<sub>ut</sub> = 700 MPa and S<sub>yt</sub> = 550 MPa. Bending at the fillet alternates between +120 MPa and −120 MPa. Find the fatigue factor of safety by the Goodman criterion and comment on the result.
outline: K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + q(K<sub>t</sub> − 1)
the cycle is fully reversed: σ<sub>m</sub> = 0, σ<sub>a</sub> = 120 MPa
K<sub>f</sub> on the alternating stress
n = S<sub>e</sub>/(K<sub>f</sub> σ<sub>a</sub>) for zero mean stress
n < 1: the fillet will fail; redesign
with a mean stress, use σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> = 1/n

answer.text: Data: K<sub>t</sub> = 2.2, q = 0.9, S<sub>e</sub> = 220 MPa (taken as already corrected for surface and size), S<sub>ut</sub> = 700 MPa, S<sub>yt</sub> = 550 MPa; bending stress at the fillet from +120 to −120 MPa (nominal).
Cycle: σ<sub>m</sub> = (120 + (−120))/2 = 0; σ<sub>a</sub> = (120 − (−120))/2 = 120 MPa. Fully reversed, R = −1, so the working point lies on the σ<sub>a</sub> axis.
Fatigue notch factor: K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + 0.9 × (2.2 − 1) = 1 + 1.08 = 2.08.
Effective alternating stress: K<sub>f</sub> σ<sub>a</sub> = 2.08 × 120 = 249.6 MPa.
Goodman with σ<sub>m</sub> = 0 reduces to 1/n = K<sub>f</sub> σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub>:

Comment. n < 1: the effective stress amplitude exceeds the endurance limit, so the shaft will crack at the fillet after a finite number of cycles. The smooth shaft would have been safe (220/120 = 1.83); the notch alone makes it fail. Static yield is not the problem: 120 MPa is far below 550 MPa.
Redesign options, worked for a target n = 1.5:

head: Change
What it needs
rows: stress must fall by 249.6 × 1.5/220 = 1.70 times; section modulus × 1.70, diameter × 1.70<sup>1/3</sup> = 1.19
K<sub>f</sub> ≤ 220/(1.5 × 120) = 1.22, so K<sub>t</sub> ≤ 1 + 0.22/0.9 = 1.25: a much larger radius or a relief groove
shot peening or rolling raises S<sub>e</sub>; combine with a larger radius

answer.text: If the cycle also had a mean stress, say σ<sub>m</sub> = 60 MPa, Goodman would give 1/n = 249.6/220 + 60/700 = 1.135 + 0.086 = 1.221, n = 0.82, still worse.

Why the notch factor goes on the alternating stress. The alternating stress drives crack initiation at the root of the fillet, where the local stress is raised; the notch sensitivity q = 0.9 says the steel feels 90 % of the theoretical rise. With σ<sub>m</sub> = 0 there is no mean term for K<sub>f</sub> to act on, so the choice between textbooks that apply K<sub>f</sub> to σ<sub>a</sub> only or to both does not matter in this question.

A word on S<sub>e</sub>. The question gives S<sub>e</sub> = 220 MPa. If this were the test-bar value 0.5S<sub>ut</sub> = 350 MPa, the Marin factors (for example k<sub>a</sub> = 0.8, k<sub>b</sub> = 0.85 for a machined 30 mm shaft, giving 238 MPa) would be applied first; 220 MPa is already of that order, so it is taken as the corrected value.
Closing check: 1/n = 249.6/220 = 1.135 → n = 0.881, below 1; after a 1.19-times larger diameter, K<sub>f</sub> σ<sub>a</sub> = 249.6/1.70 = 146.8 MPa and n = 220/146.8 = 1.50.

bank.q: Compare the maximum shear stress theory and the distortion energy theory. Show how much their yield predictions differ in pure shear, and explain why the distortion energy theory agrees better with test data for ductile metals.
outline: in pure shear σ<sub>1</sub> = τ, σ<sub>2</sub> = −τ, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0
Tresca gives τ<sub>y</sub> = 0.5 S<sub>yt</sub>
von Mises gives τ<sub>y</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>/√3 = 0.577 S<sub>yt</sub>
difference of about 15 %
hydrostatic stress does not cause yield, and only the distortion energy excludes it
Tresca is simple and safe for design; von Mises is more accurate for analysis

answer.text: Both theories for a ductile material. Tresca: failure when σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub> (maximum shear stress reaches S<sub>yt</sub>/2). Von Mises: failure when √(½[(σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>)² + (σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)² + (σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>)²]) = S<sub>yt</sub> (distortion energy reaches its tensile-test value).
Pure shear state. A shaft in pure torsion with shear stress τ has principal stresses σ<sub>1</sub> = τ, σ<sub>2</sub> = 0, σ<sub>3</sub> = −τ.
Tresca in pure shear: σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = τ − (−τ) = 2τ = S<sub>yt</sub>, so the shear yield strength is τy = 0.5S<sub>yt</sub>.
Von Mises in pure shear:
answer.pre:
½[(τ − 0)² + (0 + τ)² + (−τ − τ)²] = ½[τ² + τ² + 4τ²] = 3τ² = S<sub>yt</sub>²
τy = S<sub>yt</sub>/√3 = 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>

answer.text: Difference: 0.577/0.5 = 1.155, so von Mises allows 15.5 % more shear stress. For S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa, τy = 200 MPa (Tresca) and 231 MPa (von Mises). In uniaxial tension or equal biaxial tension both give S<sub>yt</sub>, so the gap is zero there; on a σ<sub>1</sub>–σ<sub>2</sub> plot the hexagon touches the ellipse at six corners and is widest apart on the pure-shear line.

Agreement with tests. Torsion tests on ductile steels give yield in shear at about 0.55 to 0.6S<sub>yt</sub>, close to 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>. The physical reason is that yield is slip, a change of shape: a hydrostatic stress, which only changes volume, does not cause it, and the distortion energy (and the equivalent octahedral shear stress) is exactly the part of the strain energy that leaves the hydrostatic stress out. Tresca also ignores hydrostatic stress but ignores σ<sub>2</sub> as well, so it misses the effect of the middle principal stress.
Comparison.

Octahedral shear stress view. The shear stress on the octahedral planes (equally inclined to the three principal axes) is τoct = (1/3)√((σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>)² + (σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)² + (σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>)²) = (√2/3) σ<sub>eq</sub>. So von Mises can also be read as a maximum octahedral shear stress theory: it uses all three principal stress differences, while Tresca uses only the largest one.
Closing check: for a 40 mm shaft carrying 800 N·m only, τ = 63.66 MPa and with S<sub>yt</sub> = 300 MPa, n = 150/63.66 = 2.36 by Tresca and 173.2/63.66 = 2.72 by von Mises, 15 % apart as predicted.

bank.q: Discuss the effect of mean stress on fatigue failure. Compare the Soderberg, Goodman, Gerber and yield-line criteria on a Haigh diagram, and recommend a criterion for a gearbox shaft and for a highly stressed aircraft component, giving reasons.
outline: Haigh diagram: σ<sub>a</sub> against σ<sub>m</sub>, intercepts S<sub>e</sub> and S<sub>yt</sub> or S<sub>ut</sub>
Soderberg to S<sub>yt</sub>, Goodman to S<sub>ut</sub>, Gerber a parabola to S<sub>ut</sub>
Langer line σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub> must not be crossed
Gerber fits ductile data, Goodman slightly conservative, Soderberg most conservative
compressive mean stress does not reduce life
choice depends on data, consequence of failure and checking

answer.text: Effect of mean stress. A tensile mean stress holds fatigue cracks open and adds to the peak, so the alternating stress a part can carry falls as σ<sub>m</sub> rises; at σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>ut</sub> no alternation at all can be carried. A compressive mean stress tends to close cracks and does not shorten life (it is the basis of shot peening).

Haigh diagram (sketch): σ<sub>m</sub> on the horizontal axis, σ<sub>a</sub> on the vertical. Every line starts at S<sub>e</sub> on the σ<sub>a</sub> axis (fully reversed). A working point is safe inside the line; its factor of safety is the ratio of the distance to the line along a ray from the origin to the distance of the point.
The four lines.

head: Line
Equation
Character
rows: straight to S<sub>yt</sub>; lowest; also guards yield
straight to S<sub>ut</sub>; slightly below test data
parabola to S<sub>ut</sub>; through the middle of the data
first-cycle yield; not a fatigue line

answer.text: Comparison with numbers (S<sub>e</sub> = 230, S<sub>yt</sub> = 400, S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa; σ<sub>m</sub> = 80, σ<sub>a</sub> = 40 MPa):
answer.pre: Soderberg n = 2.67   Goodman n = 3.25   Gerber n = 4.06   Langer n = 3.33

answer.text: So Soderberg is the most conservative and needs no yield check; Goodman is moderate; Gerber is closest to test data but here would let the part yield (4.06 > 3.33), so Gerber must always be paired with the Langer line, and Goodman too near the σ<sub>m</sub> axis.

Gearbox shaft. Material data (S<sub>ut</sub>, S<sub>yt</sub>, S<sub>e</sub> with Marin factors) are known, the load is well defined and the shaft is easily inspected and replaced. Recommend Goodman (or the ASME elliptic line that shaft codes use) with a yield check, at n ≈ 1.5 to 2. Soderberg would oversize the shaft; Gerber is acceptable only with Langer.

Highly stressed aircraft component. Weight matters, so Gerber or test-based curves are used to avoid needless mass, but failure is catastrophic, so the margin comes from high-reliability S<sub>e</sub> (k<sub>e</sub> at 99.9 %, 0.753), measured S–N data, a safety factor applied to life as well as stress, and inspection intervals from crack-growth analysis. If only handbook data are available, Goodman with the Langer check is the defensible choice; Soderberg would be too heavy.

Conclusion: choose the line by the quality of the data and the cost of failure; always check yield; never use a straight-line criterion for a compressive mean stress (use σ<sub>a</sub> ≤ S<sub>e</sub>/n).

bank.q: A shaft has failed in service at a keyway even though the calculated nominal stress was below yield. Analyse the possible reasons and explain how you would redesign the part.
outline: fatigue under repeated stress below yield
K<sub>t</sub> at the keyway end, converted to K<sub>f</sub> through q
rough surface, corrosion or fretting under the key
residual tensile stress from machining
bending plus torsion acting together at the same section
remedies: end-milled or sled-runner keyway, larger fillet, shot peening, induction hardening, better finish
recheck with the Goodman line and a suitable factor of safety

answer.text: Diagnosis: fatigue. A failure below yield in a rotating shaft is almost always fatigue. The fracture face would show a smooth zone with beach marks starting at the keyway corner and a rough final-fracture zone; its size shows how high the stress was.

Why at the keyway. The keyway end and its root corners are notches. An end-milled keyway has K<sub>t</sub> of about 2 in bending and higher in torsion at sharp corners; with q ≈ 0.9 for a hardened shaft steel, K<sub>f</sub> = 1 + 0.9(K<sub>t</sub> − 1) ≈ 1.9 or more, so the effective stress amplitude was about twice the calculated nominal value. The designer probably compared the nominal stress with yield, a static check, and ignored the notch.
Other contributors.

head: Cause
Effect
rows: every surface point sees a fully reversed stress each turn
adds shear; use von Mises equivalents of σ<sub>a</sub> and τ<sub>a</sub>
k<sub>a</sub> about 0.8; tool marks start cracks
micro-slip wears the surface and starts cracks
pits act as notches; no endurance limit in a wet environment
Tensile residual stress from machining or welding

answer.text: Check that should have been made: S<sub>e</sub> = k<sub>a</sub> k<sub>b</sub> k<sub>c</sub> k<sub>d</sub> k<sub>e</sub> × 0.5S<sub>ut</sub>; σ<sub>a,eq</sub> = √((K<sub>f</sub> σ<sub>a</sub>)² + 3(K<sub>fs</sub> τ<sub>a</sub>)²) and σ<sub>m,eq</sub> from the steady torque; Goodman 1/n = σ<sub>a,eq</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m,eq</sub>/S<sub>ut</sub> with n ≈ 1.5 to 2, plus a Langer yield check.

Redesign. (1) Use a sled-runner keyway (cut by a disc cutter) instead of an end-milled one, and give the keyway root a generous radius. (2) Move the keyway away from the shoulder so the two stress raisers do not add. (3) Increase the shaft diameter at that section, or the fillet radius of any nearby shoulder. (4) Improve the surface: grind, shot peen or roll the keyway area to put it in compression; induction-harden the surface. (5) Fit the hub with an interference fit or use a spline or keyless locking to reduce fretting. (6) Protect against corrosion.

Numerical illustration. A shaft with S<sub>e</sub> = 220 MPa and a nominal alternating bending stress of 120 MPa is safe as a smooth bar (n = 1.83). With K<sub>t</sub> = 2.2 and q = 0.9 at a sharp corner, K<sub>f</sub> = 2.08 and n = 220/(2.08 × 120) = 0.88: it fails. Reducing K<sub>f</sub> to 1.22 by a milder geometry and finish restores n = 220/(1.22 × 120) = 1.50.
Recheck the new design with the Goodman line and the yield line, then confirm by inspecting the first units in service.

bank.q: Explain why a load applied suddenly produces a larger stress than the same load applied gradually. Derive the impact factor for a suddenly applied load and for a weight dropped from a height, and state the assumptions made.
outline: work done by the load equals strain energy stored
gradual load: work ½Pδ, factor 1
sudden load: work Wδ = ½kδ², factor 2
dropped weight: W(h + δ) = ½kδ², δ = δ<sub>st</sub>(1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>))
assumptions: elastic, no energy lost, struck mass neglected, uniform stress
stress concentration still applies on top

answer.text: Set up: a bar (or any elastic member) of stiffness k = AE/L carries a weight W. Static extension δ<sub>st</sub> = W/k, static stress σ<sub>st</sub> = W/A. Since the bar is linear, its force is kδ and its strain energy is U = ½kδ² = σ²AL/(2E).
Gradual load. The load grows from 0 to W in step with the extension, so the work done is the triangle ½Wδ. Equating ½Wδ = ½kδ² gives δ = W/k = δ<sub>st</sub>: impact factor 1.

Suddenly applied load. The full W acts from the first instant (released from touching the collar). By the time the bar has stretched δ the weight has done work Wδ, a rectangle, but the bar stores only the triangle ½kδ²:
At this instant the bar force is 2W, twice the load: the extra work has gone into speeding the weight up, and the bar overshoots to twice the static stretch and then oscillates about δ<sub>st</sub>.
Weight dropped through h. When the bar is at its maximum stretch the weight is momentarily at rest, so all the potential energy it has lost, over the fall h and the stretch δ, is stored:
answer.pre:
W(h + δ) = ½kδ²
with W = kδst:   δ² − 2δ<sub>st</sub> δ − 2hδst = 0
δ = δ<sub>st</sub> + √(δ<sub>st</sub>² + 2hδst) = δ<sub>st</sub>(1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>))
impact factor = 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>);  σ = σ<sub>st</sub> × impact factor

answer.text: Checks on the result. At h = 0 it gives 2, the sudden load. When h ≫ δ<sub>st</sub> it tends to √(2h/δ<sub>st</sub>), so a stiff member (small δ<sub>st</sub>) suffers a large factor.

Assumptions: the material stays within its elastic limit; no energy is lost as heat, sound or local plastic flow at the point of contact; the mass of the struck member is neglected; the stress is uniform along the bar at every instant (no stress waves); the weight stays in contact after impact. Stress concentration at holes or threads still multiplies the result.

Numbers: W = 500 N on a 20 mm steel rod 1 m long, h = 50 mm: δ<sub>st</sub> = 0.007958 mm, impact factor = 1 + √(1 + 12 566) = 113.1, σ = 113.1 × 1.59 = 180 MPa. A 2000 N/mm spring on the collar raises δ<sub>st</sub> to 0.258 mm and cuts the factor to 20.7 and the rod stress to 33 MPa.

glossary.def: A material that shows large plastic strain before fracture, usually more than 5 % elongation in a tensile test.
A material that fractures with little or no plastic deformation and is stronger in compression than in tension.
The stress at which a material begins to deform permanently, measured in MPa.
The highest engineering stress reached in a tensile test, before necking begins.
A stress state in which one principal stress is zero, as on the free surface of a loaded shaft.
Equal normal stress on all three planes with no shear; it changes volume but does not make a ductile metal yield.
The shear stress on the octahedral planes, whose magnitude is proportional to the von Mises equivalent stress.
Any geometric feature such as a hole, groove, keyway or shoulder that forces the stress lines to crowd together.
The stress found from the simple axial, bending or torsion formula on the net section at a notch, ignoring the local disturbance.
A rounded transition between two sections of different size, provided to reduce the stress concentration.
The number of cycles a part survives at a given stress amplitude before it fails.
A cycle in which the stress swings equally on both sides of zero, so the stress ratio R = −1.
A cycle that rises from zero to a maximum and falls back to zero, so the stress ratio R = 0.
R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub>, the number that fixes where a cycle sits on the Haigh diagram.
A plot of alternating stress against mean stress used to check fatigue safety against a failure line.
The steady extension of a crack by a small step each cycle in stage II, roughly following the Paris law.
Correction factors for surface finish, size, load type, temperature and reliability that convert the specimen endurance limit into a component endurance limit.
The energy stored in a deformed body, equal to the area under its load–deflection curve.
The strain energy stored per unit volume at the yield point, equal to S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E).
A load that goes from zero to its full value in one step, producing twice the static deflection and stress.
The energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture, given by the whole area under the stress–strain curve.
The ratio of the strength of the part to the stress it actually carries.
A narrow band on the surface of a cyclically loaded metal where slip concentrates and a fatigue crack starts.
A fine ridge on a fatigue fracture surface that marks the advance of the crack in one load cycle.
A larger curved mark on a fatigue fracture surface showing where the crack front stood after a block of cycles.
